source.title: Neurons Speak in Ranges: Breaking Free from Discrete Neuronal Attribution
source.authors: Muhammad Umair Haider; Hammad Rizwan; Hassan Sajjad; Peizhong Ju; A. Siddique

record.file_problem: The full paper and appendices are present; no relevant cutoff or garbling noted.
record.tranche_reason: The study measures salient-neuron overlap across concepts and argues that discrete neuron-to-concept attribution misses polysemanticity. It offers a refinement, but does not count neurons by number of understandable jobs.
record.gate_note: The study reports further activation-distribution statistics and intervention results, but these do not measure the specific audit shares, explanation prediction scores, or circuit sufficiency named in the claim versions. Table 6 compares saliency methods for concept erasure; it is not a count of interpretable neuron jobs. Figure 2 provides no exact values in the text except for IMDB.
record.test_reason: The study does not count neurons by number of understandable jobs or score explanations. Its polysemanticity measure counts a hidden-state dimension as polysemantic if it is in the top-30% max-activation set for more than one task label. That is a related but different construct: it uses residual/CLS dimensions rather than MLP neuron poles, and coarse dataset labels rather than named jobs. A dimension with one coherent job can be salient for several classes. The essay's claim is not tested or used, so the findings go under fits_no_version.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors also state that polysemanticity is pervasive, even among highly salient neurons, which undermines discrete neuron–concept attribution. They add that range-based masking preserves MMLU and limits perplexity increases.
record.recipe_differences: The paper measures cross-class overlap of salient neurons and concept-conditioned activation distributions, then compares range-based and whole-neuron interventions. It does not use the original pole-level audit or explanation-rating procedure.
record.method_sensitivity: Overlap results vary by model and dataset; the study also reports that activation patterns vary by layer, with early GPT-2 layers showing more concept overlap and distinct concept-level distributions emerging around layers 5–6.

fits_no_version.finding: Top-30% max-activation salient dimensions overlap heavily across task labels: over 60% for IMDB in GPT-2; Figure 2 and Table 5 cover GPT-2, BERT and Llama-3.2-3B.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Hidden-state dimensions salient for one task label are often also salient for other labels (label-level saliency overlap).

fits_no_version.finding: Concept-conditioned activations of salient dimensions are near-Gaussian with limited overlap between concepts (Tables 1, 7, 9). Separation emerges from GPT-2 layers 5–6 onward. Range-gated ablation erases the target concept with less collateral damage than whole-dimension masking (Tables 3, 4).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Different concepts occupy separable activation ranges within a single neuron, so range-level attribution is more selective than whole-neuron attribution.

fits_no_version.finding: Range masking on Gemma Scope SAE features lowers auxiliary-concept damage versus full feature masking (Table 32); the authors read this as SAE features not being strictly monosemantic.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: SAE features also show concept mixing that range gating can separate.

record.problems: The overlap analysis uses labeled classification concepts and selected salient neurons, not an audit of all neuron poles or human-nameable jobs. The paper gives no error bars or confidence intervals for these overlap values. Figure 2's exact values are not stated in the text except for IMDB.
record.rows_left_out: No rows omitted under the 60-row limit.

untested.parts: No share of neurons with one or two jobs in any model; no mixture-of-experts models or large-scale models.
No vision models or reanalysis of canonical examples.
No comparison across architectures, regularization or tools on interpretable share.
No held-out prediction test of activating-example explanations.

record.verdict_notes: The neurons here are hidden-state (residual/CLS) dimensions at the penultimate layer or label token, not MLP neurons. Concepts are coarse dataset labels. The paper's polysemanticity counts therefore cannot be compared with the essay's job-per-pole shares. The record's V2 linkage and limits_scope label are removed.

versions.untested_parts: The study does not audit Qwen3-32B, neuron poles, or the stated one-job/two-job/not-understood percentages.

It measures overlap in salient neurons across labeled dataset classes, not the share of neurons with one or two named jobs. It does not test mixture-of-experts models or scaling up to trillions of parameters.
No InceptionV1 cat-and-car example, pose interpretation, or recursive-generalization analysis.
No comparison of architecture or regularization effects on the share of interpretable neurons, and no InceptionV1-sized vision-model estimates.
No attribution-graph test of whether a model's own neurons suffice to explain behavior.
The study does not test whether explanations built from activating examples predict firing on held-out activations.
The study does not score neuron explanations by simulated activations on new text.
